article.title: Progressives Must Rethink Race
article.author: Tom Hall
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. It’s time for Americans, including progressives, to try new thinking about race. The right-wing e-newsletter The Dispatch called the midterms “A Blowout.” The Donald’s immediate response was to double down on the politics of division and to appoint extreme racist Stephen Miller as his chief of staff for the remainder of his term. Much of the “progressive” response to the midterms has been a mixture of gloating, recriminations about the “Democratic Party Machine,” and announced plans for retribution—against both enemies and natural allies. At the October 2–4 Left Coast Forum in Los Angeles, a conservatively dressed, gray-haired gentleman with a complexion darker than Herschel Walker’s sat in the back row of several sessions. He didn’t speak most of the time, but when he did, he was soft-spoken and not confrontational. When I approached him, he identified himself as an MSW and a social policy analyst. One issue came to the fore each time I spoke to him or heard him speak during a session. He asserted that “race” is a false construct and that focusing on it risks distracting us from the real problems and issues facing society. Science has pretty well eliminated any objective basis for racial classifications. Even before European mercantilism and colonialism initiated global mass trading that mixed heretofore separate population groups and civilizations, people were people. We share essentially 100% identical DNA, regardless of individual variations in gene expression affecting eye color, skin pigmentation, perceived “beauty,” handedness, disease susceptibility, and a million other characteristics. Related: What If AI Learns That Inequality—not Humanity—is the Problem? People descended from other primates that lived in groups. And people, from their earliest manifestations, have been group-focused primates. As small groups merged into villages, then cities and states, they retained their group identities and practiced behaviors that pitted groups against other groups, both for survival and for gain. This pattern is not unique to evil Caucasian colonists trying to subjugate Africans, Asians, Latin Americans, and Native Americans. It is what history and science tell us about humans on every continent, humans of every color, and humans of every political persuasion, going back as far as archaeological remains reveal evidence of group living, group warfare, and individual violence. “Race” as a social definition is much more recent and is essentially an economic rather than a scientific or social reality. As early as 1640, a Virginia colonial court sentenced a Black man to lifetime servitude while sentencing his White co-defendants to only extended indenture. And in 1661, Virginia started crafting laws to officially recognize “race-based” slavery. These were decisions of economic policy, not scientific reality. American slavery was novel. Spain instituted slavery across the Caribbean, first trying to coerce Native Americans into providing labor as part of purported religious instruction and conversion. But Native Americans had the home-court advantage and easily disappeared into forests and jungles when they didn’t want to be slaves. Following Christopher Columbus’s example of seizing people from lands he explored, traders traveling to Africa seized Africans and brought them to the New World. The Africans didn’t have the Native Americans’ local knowledge or connections to local tribes that might have enabled them to escape bondage. And the traders had many customers eager for captive workers who had no opportunities for escape. So the 1661 Virginia slavery legislation was a formalization of an emerging economic system that used an artificial and unscientific basis for providing legal economic benefits to plantation owners. Then, a 1662 Virginia law held that “Black” children’s status followed that of their mother rather than their father. Therefore, a child born to an enslaved mother was automatically a slave, even if the child’s father was a free “White” man. By breeding their slaves, plantation owners could increase their wealth without economic investment. Monopoly capitalism at its finest. Related: Trump, Iran and the New Middle East Power Shift As European societies increasingly recognized that human slavery was entirely inconsistent with Christianity, and as Latin American colonies threw off French and Spanish colonial rule (Haiti in 1804 and Mexico in 1821), the United States doubled down on human slavery. The plantation economy of the American South was the greatest source of income for the new nation. And it depended entirely on slave labor. Although sermons and treatises defended human slavery as beneficial and “Christian,” more and more voices were raised in support of abolition. Slave owners and the governments that depended on slavery-generated income passed laws making it illegal to teach slaves to read, write, and do arithmetic. Enslaved Christian preachers were criminalized, with increasingly severe restrictions imposed after preachers like Nat Turner encouraged freedom in the name of Christianity. Leading up to the American Civil War, there was no longer any pretense. Race-based human slavery was an economic engine. In 1845, Southern plantation owners who were members of the Baptist Church in America broke away from the main Baptist organization and founded the Southern Baptist Convention (SBC). The two groups’ theology remained the same, with the exception that the SBC proclaimed that “Black” people were created inferior by God and were destined to exist in eternal servitude to the White master race. The creation of the SBC was an entirely economic move, with no pretense of any scientific basis. It was simply an announcement by wealthy plantation owners that their economic interests mandated the creation of their own new religion, rejecting the Christian teachings of both Catholic and Protestant churches around the world. The same logic underlay the creation of the Klan and all Jim Crow laws. But the economic interests were not specific to race. The successes of the labor movement in the first decades of the 20th century were limited by efforts to convince White workers to see “Black” and “Latin” workers as economic enemies. The interest was not racial separation but dissension between visibly identifiable groups of workers, keeping them from forming stronger unions that might demand bigger pieces of the industrial pie. Historians of the late 18th and early 19th centuries point to identical efforts by American diplomats negotiating with Native American tribes. While numerous diplomats recorded Native American efforts to persuade tribes to put aside their differences and consolidate their efforts to resist land takeovers in the Ohio Valley and other areas southeast of the Mississippi River, the record of treaties made and then broken consistently shows diplomats’ efforts to deal with individual tribes rather than groups (unions?) of tribes. After World War II, which followed the great economic democratizing successes of the New Deal, the Civil Rights Movement gained momentum. While many of today’s “progressives” and “revolutionaries” spout stock “Marxist” phraseology against religion, the Civil Rights Movement did what labor unions had failed to do. Churches of various denominations encouraged the involvement of all people in the struggle. Fundamentalists who believed that Catholics sided with Satan and that Jews killed Jesus agreed to work with Catholics and Jews to end segregation. Looking at innumerable civil rights activities, we focus on a few heroic women, such as Rosa Parks and Mamie Till-Mobley. The movement was built on the labor of women before there was a Women’s Movement. It was built on the work of nuns, the efforts of women working in Jewish congregations and Protestant churches, women performers spreading messages of freedom, and the work of women who, decades earlier, had developed tactics and messages for women’s suffrage. Related: From Bull Connor to ICE: The Return of State-Sanctioned Violence The Women’s Movement met as much resistance as the Labor Movement had, albeit with less overt violence, from the same forces that, in the 1930s, 1950s, and the 1960s, had opposed every other effort to get working people to see themselves first as working people with common interests, rather than as people with different skin tones, national and religious backgrounds, or differently formed eyelids. In a rejection, even a denial, of science, firefighters and police officers were encouraged to resist the inclusion of women in their “male” professions. And the same foolishness continues today as the nation’s secretary of defense rails that women can’t perform in leadership roles or in combat, even as every modern nation around the world has successfully integrated women into its war machine. The same secretary, for the same divide-and-conquer reasons, is denying qualified “Black” and “Brown” men promotions and positions of authority. It’s easy to see why corporations that thrive on low-paid labor and those that suck down tax dollars for unproven weaponry want to promote divisive thinking. Billions of dollars are at stake in every budget year. No one wants to give money to workers instead of allocating it to management bonuses and shareholder dividends. But it is our tax money. It is our consumer money. Discrimination against Asians, Blacks, Latinos, and Native Americans has never been about race. It has been about economic advantages. Cheap Chinese and Irish laborers were both imported to build our railroads. Both were called “inferior,” while the corporations that imported them really meant “cheaper.” There were times when Eastern Europeans and Southern Europeans were imported as cheaper and supposedly “inferior” workers. Hungarians and other Eastern Europeans (collectively disparaged as “Hunkies”) filled steel mills. Italians (“Wops”) filled cheap factory and agricultural jobs. The use of derogatory nicknames helped—and continues to help—maintain their categorization as separate from and inferior to “real Americans.” In the 1640 Virginia case involving John Punch, racial distinctions that had no meaning for the defendants were beneficial to businessmen. Three men, all indentured to Hugh Glyn, ran away from Virginia but were captured in Maryland. They were punished for fleeing from indentured servitude. John Punch was a “Black” servant. The two runaways with him were “White.” The two White runaways were sentenced to longer periods of indenture. John Punch was sentenced to lifetime servitude. Racism is not a natural phenomenon. Running away from slavery was a regular feature of life in the American colonies. And although Africans generally had darker skin tones than Native Americans, runaway slaves were often accepted and adopted into Native American clans and families. Related: Privatize the Profits, Socialize the Costs But racism can be learned. As colonial intrusion shrank Native American communities, those communities tried to find ways to resist, fight back, and reclaim lands taken from them by settlers moving west from the growing United States. The Cherokee Nation tried to model its government on that of the United States, developing its own written language, writing a constitution, and forming a bicameral legislature and a judiciary independent of executive functions. The Cherokees had prospered economically. They built plantations and exported cotton and other crops to the United States. They worked their plantations with slave labor, even while incorporating free “Black” people into Cherokee families and communities. But when the Cherokee Constitution was adopted in 1827, it explicitly disenfranchised “Black” people, including the “Black”-fathered children of Cherokee women. To succeed in business relations with their dominant neighbor, Cherokees learned to adopt American racism after having been welcoming to “Black” people fleeing slavery for more than two centuries. Similarly, both French and Spanish legal systems recognized property ownership and legal personhood for women. Women could buy, inherit, manage, and sell their own property. But when the United States took over French and Spanish territories, it imposed English “common law,” under which a woman’s property became her husband’s and her legal personhood was subsumed into his. There were no biological or other scientific reasons for this. It was simply a feudal system that concentrated financial control in limited hands. The experiences of indentured servants, Native Americans abandoning traditional societal inclusiveness, workers trying to organize, and women trying to live in their respective societies each teach us that scientific realities can be overcome by social training. The Labor Movement, Civil Rights Movement, Women’s Rights Movement, and Gay Rights Movement all teach us that training can move societies away from artificial bigotries. The forces of economic self-interest will always push divisiveness. It is in their interest to increase conflict and pit their workers and customers against each other. The fear of losing a job opportunity to another applicant is similar to the fear of losing the last Cabbage Patch doll to another customer in the holiday rush. Pushing fear as a marketing technique to increase profit is natural. It is as old as competing preachers proclaiming that they each have access to the only eternal truths. But let us not solely blame businessmen and the defenders of social “traditions.” As the October Left Coast Forum also showed us, “leftist” organizations have their own traditions of divisive thinking. Marxists point out the dogmatic purity of Leninists, who disdain backsliders and people who differ over points of dogma. And “everybody” hates the Trotskyites. It is easy to find “progressives” who are eager to attack their allies over details of policies on which they nominally agree. “Race” is one of those policies. For many progressives, accepting the traditional, conservative definition that racial distinctions exist is their natural starting point. After all, they have learned all their lives that race exists and that race matters. They “know” that it’s real because they’ve experienced its effects all their lives. Changing that thinking will not stop those who benefit from racism from continuing to practice it, continuing to promote it, and continuing to benefit from it. But changing the training can, has, and will disrupt the efforts of bigots and profiteers and move society toward further abandoning the artifices created by colonial businessmen in the early 17th century. The Cherokee National Constitution of 1827 didn’t prevent the forced military removal of the Cherokee Nation from its land under Andrew Jackson. But years later, the Cherokee removed the explicitly racist, exclusionary language. If those whom our Founding Fathers called “the savage Indians” could learn to adopt and then abandon artificial constructs, shouldn’t we “superior” modern people be able to learn at least as well? Related: AI, the Bible, and the Battle Over Who Controls Knowledge President Obama delivered a speech on his racial position and got himself elected president of the United States. He delivered the long-overdue beginnings of a national healthcare program, which led to his condemnation by both racist, pro-business healthcare backers and “progressives” who thought he didn’t deliver enough, despite the strident and staunch opposition embodied in Mitch McConnell’s “one-term president” decree. The 16th Amendment moved the needle. It didn’t make our tax system fair, just fairer. The 19th Amendment gave women the vote. It didn’t make all women vote sensibly, any more than male suffrage makes MAGA men vote sensibly. The failure of the Equal Rights Amendment did not stop the development of the Women’s Movement or the great (if still inadequate) strides toward equality for women. The same can and must be said of race. Race is an artificial construct, created and maintained for the benefit of economically controlling interests. It has no objective reality. But it enjoys widespread belief and acceptance. A proper progressive response to racial discrimination in our society is not to continue to accept it as “reality” but rather to begin to attack the fake construct itself and work to rob it of its social acceptance. Exploiting racial themes for fundraising and political leverage is effective. We have increasingly diverse representation at all levels of government. People seeking government services encounter government employees from an increasingly broad range of ethnicities, religions, and national origins, all to the benefit of society. Exposing pernicious racism when it presents itself remains a necessary part of the process. It leads to progress. We need to find new language for talking about “race”—new language that is not grounded in acceptance of conservative and business-centered divisiveness, definitions, and terminology. New language that can speak both to progressives and to those who are coming to see that their support for the Donald and for corporate oligarchy was misplaced and self-injuring. It won’t be easy, but new language can help us develop a new construct about “race,” a new understanding that it isn’t real. Working out new language will be messy, as all important social progress is. We learned in the early 20th century to “dial” our telephones. How many of today’s children “dial” their cell phones without any idea of what the term even means? What verb will emerge to refer to the process of mechanical arms reaching out to catch descending rocket ships, replacing the long sentence used by SpaceX to describe its new process of handling returning spaceships? Race itself was once a new term. François Bernier, a French physician, proposed dividing humans into four races back in 1684, 44 years after John Punch was sentenced to lifetime servitude. Ignoring the fact that it took some years for Dr. Bernier’s idea to spread widely, 342 years is long enough for his faulty concept to be abandoned. But it should take many, many fewer years to convince Americans to abandon it, as so much of the rest of civilization has. Related: Young Blood Isn’t Enough—and Neither Is Experience The midterm elections were a wake-up call, showing that American voters are frustrated and open to change. But open to what change? Republicans, with their embrace of the Donald’s appointment of Stephen Miller and their defense of Pete Hegseth, have shown their intractability. What of progressives? Can they rethink their commitment to conservative, economically driven definitions of race? Can they meet the voters’ challenge to change old, stale, economically devastating definitions and assumptions? Can they learn to abandon false but profitable language for a new construct—a world that denies the false construct?
